question: What is @PathVariable in Spring MVC?
title: @PathVariable in Spring MVC — Extracting URL Path Segments
direct_answer: @PathVariable extracts a value from a URL path template variable. In @GetMapping("/users/{id}"), the {id} part is extracted from the actual URL and bound to the annotated parameter. Used for resource identification in REST APIs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of REST URL parameter extraction and how Spring MVC binds path segments to method parameters
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @RequestParam for resource identifiers like user ID instead of @PathVariable, which breaks REST conventions and makes URLs look like /users?id=42 instead of /users/42
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the REST design principle that path variables represent resource identity (the 'what') while query params represent filtering or options (the 'how')

sections.title: Path Variables in REST URLs
sections.content:
**@PathVariable** is a Spring MVC annotation that extracts dynamic values from the URL path itself and binds them to method parameters in your controller.

Think of it like capturing the house number from a street address — the URL structure defines placeholders (like `/users/{id}/orders/{orderId}`), and Spring extracts the actual values when a request comes in. This is the **primary way to identify resources** in RESTful APIs. When a client hits `GET /users/42`, Spring sees the `{id}` template variable in your `@GetMapping("/users/{id}")` mapping, extracts `42` from that position in the URL, and passes it to your method parameter annotated with `@PathVariable`. This follows REST conventions where the URL path represents the **noun** (what resource you're working with) and path variables specify **which instance** of that resource. It's built into the Java Servlet API through `HttpServletRequest` path matching, but Spring abstracts away the manual parsing with this annotation.

sections.title: @PathVariable at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|@PathVariable|~From the URL path|/users/{id} to id|part of resource identity|required by default
blue|Binding|~Template to parameter|name must match {placeholder}|or @PathVariable("id")|type-converted automatically
emerald|Use for|~Identifying a resource|/orders/42|hierarchical paths|RESTful style
rose|Trap|~Missing path segment|/users/ with no id|gives 404, not null|path variables are mandatory

sections.title: Extracting User ID from URL Path
When to Use Path Variables
sections.content:
Use **@PathVariable** when the value represents a **resource identifier** or a mandatory part of the resource hierarchy. For example, `GET /users/{userId}` to retrieve a specific user, `DELETE /products/{productId}` to remove a product, or `GET /customers/{customerId}/invoices/{invoiceId}` for nested resources. Path variables are **required by default** — if the URL doesn't match the template, Spring returns 404.

Use them when the parameter is **not optional** and defines which resource you're operating on.

Avoid using them for filtering, sorting, or pagination — those belong in query parameters. A good rule: if removing the value makes the URL meaningless (like `/users/` with no ID), it should be a path variable.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @RequestParam for resource IDs**: Freshers often write `@GetMapping("/users")` with `@RequestParam Long id`, resulting in `/users?id=42` instead of the RESTful `/users/42`. This breaks REST conventions and makes URLs harder to read and cache.
- **Forgetting type conversion errors**: If a client sends `/users/abc` where `abc` can't convert to `Long`, Spring throws `MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException`. Freshers forget to handle this with `@ExceptionHandler` and return a proper 400 Bad Request.
- **Naming mismatches**: When the path variable name differs from the parameter name, you must specify it: `@PathVariable("userId") Long id`. Freshers forget the annotation parameter and get binding errors.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@PathVariable**: extracts values from URL path segments defined in curly braces like /users/{id}
**REST convention**: path variables identify resources (nouns), query params filter or modify behavior (adjectives)
**Required by default**: if the path variable is missing, Spring returns 404 Not Found automatically
**Type conversion**: Spring converts path variables to method parameter types (String to Long, String to UUID, etc.)
**Multiple variables**: you can have several path variables in one URL like /users/{userId}/posts/{postId}
**Naming**: if the variable name differs from parameter name, use @PathVariable("name") to specify the mapping
**URL encoding**: path variables are automatically URL-decoded by Spring, so spaces become %20 in the URL but arrive as spaces in your code

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At PathVariable is a Spring annotation that extracts values directly from the URL path. When you define a mapping like at-GetMapping slash-users-slash-open-brace-id-close-brace, the part inside the braces is a placeholder. Spring pulls the actual value from that position in the URL and injects it into your method parameter. So if a client requests GET slash-users-slash-42, Spring extracts 42 and passes it to the parameter you've annotated with at-PathVariable. This is the standard way to identify resources in REST APIs. You use path variables for mandatory identifiers, like user ID or product ID, because they represent which specific resource you're working with. It's different from query parameters, which come after the question mark and are usually optional filters. A common mistake freshers make is using at-RequestParam for IDs, which results in URLs like slash-users-question-mark-id-equals-42. That's not RESTful. The REST design rule is simple: path variables are for the resource identity, the what. Query params are for options, the how. If you can't remove the value without making the URL meaningless, it should be a path variable. For example, slash-users-slash-42 identifies a user. Without the 42, the URL doesn't point to anything specific. That's your signal to use at-PathVariable.

question: What is @RequestParam in Spring MVC and when do you use it?
title: @RequestParam in Spring MVC — Query String Parameter Binding
direct_answer: @RequestParam extracts parameters from the URL query string (after the question mark). Example: /users?status=ACTIVE&page=0. Use it for optional filters, pagination, and search parameters. Supports required=false and defaultValue for optional params.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of query string parameter binding, which is essential for building list and search endpoints in real applications
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Making all @RequestParam fields required without default values, causing 400 errors when clients omit optional filtering parameters
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a realistic pagination or filtering example with required=false and defaultValue, demonstrating understanding of optional API design

sections.title: Query String Parameters in Spring MVC
sections.content:
**@RequestParam** is a Spring annotation that extracts values from the **query string** — the part of the URL that comes after the question mark (`?`).

Think of it like the options you select on a filter sidebar when shopping online: they refine what you see but don't change what product page you're on. Query params look like `/products?category=electronics&minPrice=100&sort=price`. Each `key=value` pair is separated by `&`. Spring parses this query string and binds each parameter to method arguments annotated with **@RequestParam**. This is how you build **flexible APIs** that support filtering, sorting, pagination, and search without creating dozens of different endpoints. Query parameters are **optional by nature** in HTTP, but Spring makes them required by default unless you specify `required=false` or provide a `defaultValue`. The annotation handles **type conversion** automatically — if your parameter is an `Integer`, Spring converts the string `"10"` from the URL into the number `10`. It's the backbone of every search and list endpoint in REST APIs.

sections.title: @RequestParam at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|@RequestParam|~From the query string|/users?status=ACTIVE|after the question mark|filters + pagination
blue|Options|~required + defaultValue|required=false for optional|defaultValue for a fallback|avoids missing-param errors
emerald|Use for|~Optional inputs|search, sort, page/size|not resource identity|key=value pairs
rose|Trap|~Required param missing|400 Bad Request|set required=false|or provide defaultValue

sections.title: User Search with Filtering and Pagination
When to Use Request Parameters
sections.content:
Use **@RequestParam** for **optional filtering, sorting, and pagination** in list endpoints. For example, `GET /products?category=books&minPrice=10&maxPrice=50` lets clients filter products without requiring a different endpoint for each filter combination.

Use it for **search queries** like `GET /users/search?email=john@example.com`.

Use it for **configuration options** that modify behavior, like `GET /reports?format=PDF&includeCharts=true`. Query parameters are perfect when the value is **optional or has a sensible default**. For pagination, always use `defaultValue` so clients can call `GET /users` without specifying `page=0&size=20` every time.

Avoid using query params for **resource identifiers** — that's what path variables are for. If the parameter fundamentally changes which resource you're accessing, it belongs in the path, not the query string.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Making all params required**: Freshers write `@RequestParam String status` without `required=false`, so clients must always provide every parameter or get a 400 error. This breaks flexibility — optional filters should be optional. Use `required=false` or `defaultValue` to avoid this.
- **Forgetting type conversion errors**: If a client sends `page=abc` and your parameter is `int`, Spring throws `MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException`. Freshers don't handle this with an exception handler, returning a confusing 500 instead of a clear 400.
- **Not using defaultValue for pagination**: Writing `@RequestParam int page` without a default means clients must always specify page numbers. Use `defaultValue="0"` so `GET /users` works without query params and still returns the first page.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@RequestParam**: extracts values from the URL query string after the question mark like /users?status=ACTIVE
**required attribute**: set to false to make a parameter optional (Spring injects null if missing)
**defaultValue attribute**: provides a fallback value when the parameter is absent, implicitly makes it optional
**Type conversion**: Spring automatically converts query string values to method parameter types (String to Integer, String to Boolean, etc.)
**Multiple parameters**: separate with ampersand in URL like /products?category=books&sort=price&page=0
**Use cases**: filtering, sorting, pagination, search queries — anything that modifies or refines the result set
**REST convention**: query params are for adjectives (how to filter/sort), path variables are for nouns (which resource)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At RequestParam extracts parameters from the query string, which is the part of the URL after the question mark. So if you have GET slash-users-question-mark-status-equals-ACTIVE-and-page-equals-zero, Spring pulls out status and page and binds them to your method parameters. You use this for filtering, sorting, pagination, and search. Basically anything that's optional or modifies the result set. By default, at-RequestParam fields are required. If the client doesn't send them, Spring returns a 400 error. That's usually too strict for filters. You make them optional by setting required equals false. Then Spring injects null if the parameter is missing. Or you can provide a default value with defaultValue equals quote-zero-quote. That's the pattern for pagination. You'd write at-RequestParam with defaultValue equals quote-zero-quote int page. Now clients can call GET slash-users without any query params and it still works, defaulting to page zero. A common mistake freshers make is requiring all query parameters without defaults. That forces clients to always provide every filter, even when they don't need them. The right approach is making filters optional and pagination parameters have defaults. Another thing to remember is the difference from path variables. Query params are for the how — how to filter or sort the results. Path variables are for the what — which specific resource you're accessing. If it's optional or can have a default, it's probably a query param.

question: What is the difference between @PathVariable and @RequestParam?
title: @PathVariable vs @RequestParam — URL Path vs Query String
direct_answer: @PathVariable extracts values from the URL path (e.g., /users/42 where 42 is the ID). @RequestParam extracts values from the query string (e.g., /users?status=ACTIVE). PathVariable is for resource identity; RequestParam is for optional filters and options.

interviewer_intent.testing: REST API design understanding — this is a classic comparison question that reveals whether a candidate knows RESTful URL conventions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @RequestParam for resource IDs that should be @PathVariable, resulting in non-RESTful URLs like /users?id=42 instead of /users/42
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Articulate the REST design principle: path for nouns and resource identity, query for adjectives and filtering or modification

sections.title: Two Ways to Pass Data in URLs
sections.content:
**@PathVariable** and **@RequestParam** are both Spring annotations for extracting data from URLs, but they target **different parts** of the URL and serve different purposes. **@PathVariable** pulls values from the **path itself** — the hierarchical structure before any question mark. For example, in `/users/42/orders/100`, the numbers `42` and `100` are path variables. **@RequestParam** pulls values from the **query string** — the key-value pairs after the question mark, like `/users?status=ACTIVE&page=0`.

The key difference is **semantic**: path variables identify **which resource** you're working with (the noun), while query parameters specify **how to filter or modify** the result (the adjective). This distinction comes from REST design principles. When you use path variables, you're navigating a resource hierarchy. When you use query params, you're providing options or filters. Understanding this split is critical for designing clean, RESTful APIs that follow HTTP conventions.

sections.title: @PathVariable vs @RequestParam
sections.content:
amber|@PathVariable|~Resource identity|/users/42|part of the path|usually required
blue|@RequestParam|~Filter / option|/users?status=ACTIVE|query string|often optional
emerald|Rule of thumb|~Path = which resource|query = how to filter it|/orders/9?expand=items|combine both freely
rose|Trap|~Swapping them|filters in path = ugly URLs|ids in query = non-RESTful|pick by meaning

sections.title: @PathVariable vs @RequestParam in Code
When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content:
Use **@PathVariable** when the value **identifies a specific resource** or represents a mandatory part of the resource hierarchy. Examples: `GET /users/{userId}` to fetch one user, `DELETE /products/{productId}` to remove a product, `GET /departments/{deptId}/employees/{empId}` for nested resources. If removing the value makes the URL incomplete or meaningless, it's a path variable.

Use **@RequestParam** when the value is an **optional filter, sorting rule, or pagination parameter**. Examples: `GET /users?status=ACTIVE&role=ADMIN` to filter users, `GET /products?sort=price&order=DESC` to sort results, `GET /orders?page=2&size=20` for pagination. If the parameter refines or modifies the result set but doesn't change which resource you're addressing, it's a query param. A practical rule: path variables are for **navigating to a resource**, query params are for **customizing the response**.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @RequestParam for IDs**: Freshers write `@GetMapping("/users") getUserById(@RequestParam Long id)`, resulting in `/users?id=42`. This breaks REST conventions. Resource IDs should be in the path: `/users/42` with `@PathVariable`.
- **Mixing them incorrectly**: Using path variables for filters like `/users/ACTIVE/ADMIN` instead of `/users?status=ACTIVE&role=ADMIN`. Path variables force a rigid hierarchy; query params give flexibility.
- **Not understanding required defaults**: Both annotations require parameters by default, but the failure mode differs — missing path variables return 404, missing query params return 400. Freshers don't anticipate this when designing APIs that should accept optional filters.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Location difference**: PathVariable extracts from path segments like /users/42, RequestParam extracts from query string like /users?id=42
**Semantic purpose**: PathVariable for resource identity (which resource), RequestParam for filtering and options (how to customize)
**REST convention**: path variables are nouns (users, products, orders), query params are adjectives (status, sort, page)
**Required by default**: both require values by default but fail differently — PathVariable returns 404, RequestParam returns 400
**URL design**: path variables create hierarchical resource structures, query params add optional modifiers without changing the resource
**Flexibility**: query params can be combined freely (/users?status=ACTIVE&role=ADMIN&page=0), path variables create fixed hierarchies
**Multiple values**: both support multiple extractions in one method, like @PathVariable userId and @RequestParam String status

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The key difference is where they pull data from in the URL. At PathVariable extracts values from the path itself, before any question mark. So in GET slash-users-slash-42, the 42 is a path variable. At RequestParam extracts values from the query string, after the question mark. Like GET slash-users-question-mark-status-equals-ACTIVE, where status is a request param. But it's not just about location. There's a semantic difference that's really important for REST design. Path variables represent resource identity. They tell you which resource you're working with. Like slash-users-slash-42 means user number 42. Query params represent filtering or options. They modify how you see the resource. Like slash-users-question-mark-status-equals-ACTIVE filters the user list. A simple rule is path variables are nouns, query params are adjectives. If you're navigating to a specific thing, use a path variable. If you're filtering or sorting a collection, use a query param. A common mistake freshers make is using at-RequestParam for IDs. They write slash-users-question-mark-id-equals-42, which is not RESTful. The ID should be in the path. Another difference is how they fail. If a path variable is missing, Spring returns 404 because the URL doesn't match any route. If a required query param is missing, Spring returns 400 because it's a bad request. Both are required by default, but you'd almost always make query params optional with required equals false or defaultValue, because they're filters. You'd rarely make path variables optional because they identify the resource itself.

question: How do you make @RequestParam optional with a default value?
title: Optional @RequestParam with defaultValue in Spring MVC
direct_answer: Set required=false to make a @RequestParam optional (Spring injects null if missing). Set defaultValue="value" to provide a fallback value when the parameter is absent — this also implicitly makes the parameter optional.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical API design knowledge — understanding how to build flexible endpoints that don't force clients to provide every parameter
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not setting defaults for pagination parameters, forcing clients to always specify page and size instead of having sensible defaults like page=0 and size=20
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a complete pagination example with defaultValue for both page and size, demonstrating production-ready API design

sections.title: Making Query Parameters Optional
sections.content:
By default, **@RequestParam** parameters are **required** — if a client doesn't provide them, Spring throws `MissingServletRequestParameterException` and returns **400 Bad Request**. This is too strict for most real-world APIs where filters, sorting, and pagination should be optional.

Spring provides two ways to make query parameters optional. First, set **`required=false`** in the annotation: `@RequestParam(required=false) String status`. Now if the client omits `status`, Spring injects `null` into your method parameter instead of throwing an error. Second, provide a **`defaultValue`**: `@RequestParam(defaultValue="0") int page`. When the client doesn't send `page`, Spring uses `0` instead of `null`. The `defaultValue` approach is **cleaner for pagination and sorting** because you avoid null checks — the parameter always has a value. Note that `defaultValue` **implicitly sets `required=false`**, so you don't need both. This pattern is essential for building flexible REST APIs where clients can call `GET /users` without any query params and still get a reasonable response (like the first page of all users).

sections.title: Making @RequestParam Optional
sections.content:
amber|required=false|~Makes it optional|null if absent|no 400 error|handle null yourself
blue|defaultValue|~Fallback value|implies required=false|"0" for page|"10" for size
emerald|Optional<T>|~Type-safe absence|Optional<String> param|no null checks|cleaner code
rose|Trap|~Primitive + missing|int with no value|throws on null|use Integer or defaultValue

sections.title: Optional Filters and Pagination with Defaults
When to Use Optional Parameters
sections.content:
Use **`required=false`** when the parameter is a **truly optional filter** with no sensible default. For example, `@RequestParam(required=false) String email` in a user search — if not provided, you search all users; if provided, you filter by email. The parameter being `null` is meaningful: it means "don't filter by this field." Use **`defaultValue`** when the parameter has a **sensible default value** that makes the API work without client input. This is the pattern for **pagination** (`page=0`, `size=20`), **sorting** (`sortBy="id"`, `order="ASC"`), and **boolean flags** (`includeInactive=false`). Default values make your API **easier to use** — clients can call `GET /users` and get the first 20 users without specifying `?page=0&size=20`.

Avoid making **search or filter strings** have default values like `defaultValue=""` — an empty string is different from `null` and might cause unexpected behavior in your repository layer.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **No defaults for pagination**: Freshers write `@RequestParam int page, @RequestParam int size` without `defaultValue`, forcing clients to always specify pagination. This makes simple requests like `GET /users` fail with 400. Always provide defaults for page (usually `0`) and size (usually `10` or `20`).
- **Using empty string as default**: Writing `@RequestParam(defaultValue="") String name` means `name` is never `null`, it's an empty string when omitted. This can break repository queries that check `if (name != null)`. Use `required=false` instead and handle `null` explicitly.
- **Primitive types with required=false**: Writing `@RequestParam(required=false) int page` doesn't work — primitives can't be `null`. Spring will throw an error if the parameter is missing. Use `Integer` (boxed type) instead: `@RequestParam(required=false) Integer page`, or use `defaultValue` with the primitive type.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **required=false**: makes the parameter optional, Spring injects null if the client doesn't provide it
**defaultValue**: provides a fallback value when parameter is absent, implicitly makes it optional (no need for required=false)
**Pagination pattern**: always use defaultValue for page and size so clients can call endpoints without query params
**Primitive vs boxed**: required=false doesn't work with primitive types like int — use Integer or provide a defaultValue
**null vs empty string**: defaultValue equals quote-quote gives an empty string, not null — be careful with string parameters
**Combining attributes**: you can use both required=false and defaultValue, but defaultValue alone is usually sufficient
**400 error prevention**: proper use of optional params prevents MissingServletRequestParameterException and improves API usability

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: There are two ways to make an at-RequestParam optional in Spring. First, you set required equals false. So you'd write at-RequestParam with required equals false, String status. Now if the client doesn't send the status parameter, Spring injects null instead of throwing an error. This is useful for filters that are truly optional. Second, you provide a defaultValue. Like at-RequestParam with defaultValue equals quote-zero-quote, int page. When the client omits the page parameter, Spring uses zero as the value. The nice thing about defaultValue is it implicitly makes the parameter optional, so you don't need to set required equals false as well. This is the standard pattern for pagination. You'd write at-RequestParam defaultValue equals quote-zero-quote for page and defaultValue equals quote-twenty-quote for size. Now clients can call GET slash-users without any query params and still get the first page with twenty results. That's much better than forcing them to always specify page and size. One thing to watch out for is primitive types with required equals false. If you write at-RequestParam with required equals false, int page, it won't work because primitives can't be null. You'd need to use the boxed type Integer instead, or just use defaultValue with the primitive. A common mistake freshers make is not providing defaults for pagination parameters. They make page and size required, so every single API call has to include question-mark-page-equals-zero-and-size-equals-twenty. That's annoying for clients. Always give sensible defaults for pagination, sorting, and anything that has an obvious fallback value.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: There are two ways to make a @RequestParam optional. Set required=false and Spring injects null when the parameter is absent. Or set defaultValue with a string value and Spring uses that as the fallback.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: defaultValue is usually the cleaner choice because it means you never have to check for null in your method body. The parameter always has a value — either from the client or from the default. Pagination especially benefits from this.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: defaultValue='0': page parameter defaults to the first page if not supplied.
required=false with Integer: nameFilter is null when absent — check before using.
Optional<String>: Java Optional works too — Optional.empty() when the parameter is absent.
Both approaches make the parameter optional — the difference is null vs a default value.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: sharp edge: defaultValue is always a String, even if your parameter type is int or Long. Spring converts it. But if your defaultValue string can't be parsed to the parameter type — like defaultValue='none' for an int parameter — you'll get a TypeMismatchException at request time, not startup.

speakable_v2.cap: Validate the size parameter with @Max to prevent clients from requesting thousands of records in one call — ?size=99999 is a real attack vector.

question: What is @RequestParam with a List type in Spring MVC?
title: @RequestParam List — Multi-Value Query Parameters in Spring
direct_answer: Declaring at-Request-Param List of String ids allows clients to pass multiple values for the same parameter name: slash-items-question-mark-ids-equals-one-ampersand-ids-equals-two-ampersand-ids-equals-three. Spring automatically binds all ids values into the List. You can also use comma-separated format with at-Request-Param String array ids.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of multi-value query parameter binding in Spring MVC — shows understanding beyond single-value parameters
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing at-Request-Param can bind to List or array — freshers try to manually parse a comma-separated string
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate both repeated parameter style and comma-separated style with actual code examples showing the difference

sections.title: Multi-Value Query Parameters with List Binding
sections.content:
Spring MVC supports **multi-value query parameters** where the same parameter name appears multiple times in the URL, or values are comma-separated. When you declare `@RequestParam List<String> ids`, Spring automatically collects all values into the List. This is crucial for **bulk operations** like filtering by multiple categories, selecting multiple items, or batch processing. The client can send `/api/products?ids=1&ids=2&ids=3` (repeated parameter style) or `/api/products?ids=1,2,3` (comma-separated style). Spring handles both formats.

Think of it like selecting multiple checkboxes in a web form — the form submits the same field name multiple times with different values. Without this feature, you'd have to manually parse a single string parameter and split it yourself, which is error-prone and verbose. The **List binding** keeps your controller code clean and type-safe. You can also use `String[]` or `Set<String>` depending on whether you need duplicates or not.

sections.title: @RequestParam with List
sections.content:
amber|List binding|~Repeated parameter|?ids=1&ids=2&ids=3|maps to List<String>|multi-select filters
blue|Comma form|~Single value split|?ids=1,2,3|also binds to a List|Spring splits on comma
emerald|Use for|~Bulk filters|tags, categories|batch lookups|/items?ids=...
rose|Trap|~Empty parameter|?ids= with no value|empty or [""]|set required=false

sections.title: Multi-Value Parameter Binding Examples
When to Use List-Type Request Parameters
sections.content:
Use `List<T>` parameters for **bulk operations** where clients need to select or filter by multiple values: `/api/orders?status=PENDING&status=PROCESSING` to fetch orders in multiple states. It's essential for **batch endpoints** like deleting multiple items: `DELETE /api/items?ids=1&ids=2&ids=3`.

Use it for **multi-select filters** in search or reporting endpoints: `/api/sales?regions=North&regions=South&regions=East` where users can pick multiple regions. For **tag-based filtering**, List parameters are natural: `/api/articles?tags=java&tags=spring&tags=rest`. If you need **unique values only**, use `Set<String>` instead of `List<String>` — Spring will automatically deduplicate. For **primitive types**, use boxed types (`List<Long>` not `List<long>`) because Spring's type conversion works with wrapper classes.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Manually parsing comma-separated strings**: Freshers often declare `@RequestParam String ids` then split it with `ids.split(",")`. Spring can bind to List directly — no manual parsing needed. Just use `@RequestParam List<String> ids` and it handles both repeated params and comma-separated values.
- **Using primitive arrays**: Writing `@RequestParam long[] ids` causes type conversion issues. Use boxed types: `@RequestParam List<Long> ids` or `@RequestParam Long[] ids`. Spring's conversion works better with wrapper classes.
- **Forgetting required=false for optional lists**: If the parameter is optional, you must set `@RequestParam(required = false) List<String> categories`, otherwise Spring throws an exception when the param is missing. Then check for null or empty in your code before using the list.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **List binding**: at-Request-Param List of String automatically collects multiple values from repeated parameters or comma-separated format
**Repeated parameter style**: slash-items-question-mark-ids-equals-one-ampersand-ids-equals-two sends multiple values with same parameter name
**Comma-separated style**: slash-items-question-mark-ids-equals-one-comma-two-comma-three also works with List binding
**Array alternative**: at-Request-Param String array ids works similarly but returns an array instead of a List
**Set for uniqueness**: Use Set of String to automatically deduplicate values if duplicates don't make sense
**Boxed types**: Always use List of Long or List of Integer, not primitive types like long or int
**Optional parameters**: Add required equals false if the list parameter is optional, then null-check before using

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When you declare at-Request-Param with a List type like List of String ids, Spring automatically binds multiple values from the query string into that list. The client can send the same parameter name multiple times, like slash-products-question-mark-ids-equals-one-ampersand-ids-equals-two-ampersand-ids-equals-three, and Spring collects all three values into your list. You can also use comma-separated format like ids-equals-one-comma-two-comma-three, and Spring handles that too. This is super useful for bulk operations or multi-select filters. For example, if you're building a delete endpoint that removes multiple items, you'd use at-Delete-Mapping with at-Request-Param List of Long ids, and clients can pass all the IDs they want to delete in one request. You can also use String array instead of List if you prefer arrays, or Set of String if you want automatic deduplication. One mistake freshers make is manually parsing a comma-separated string. They'll declare at-Request-Param String ids and then split it themselves. You don't need to do that — just use List, and Spring does the parsing for you. Another gotcha is forgetting to add required equals false if the parameter is optional. If you don't, Spring throws an error when the param is missing. Then in your method, check if the list is null or empty before using it. This feature keeps your controller code clean and type-safe, especially when dealing with batch operations or complex filtering scenarios.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: Declaring @RequestParam with a List type lets clients pass the same parameter name multiple times. If a client sends ?ids=1&ids=2&ids=3, Spring collects all three values into the List automatically and converts each element to the right type.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: This is the clean way to handle batch lookups — like fetching multiple items by ID in a single request. Without it, you'd receive a single string with all values and have to split it manually.

question: How do you design RESTful URLs with path variables?
title: RESTful URL Design with Path Variables — Best Practices
direct_answer: RESTful URLs use nouns (not verbs), hierarchical path variables for resource identity, and HTTP methods for actions. Example: GET /users/{id}, POST /users, DELETE /users/{id}/orders/{orderId}. The path variables identify which resource; the HTTP method defines the action.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of REST principles and URL design conventions — shows thinking beyond just Spring annotations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using verbs in URLs like /getUser or /deleteOrder — REST uses HTTP methods for actions, not URL verbs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the complete CRUD URL design for a resource hierarchy with proper HTTP methods and nested resources

sections.title: REST URL Design Principles with Path Variables
sections.content:
RESTful URLs follow a **resource-oriented** design where the URL identifies **what** (the resource) and the HTTP method defines **how** (the action). Path variables like `/users/{userId}` represent the **unique identifier** of a resource instance.

The key principle: URLs are **nouns**, never verbs. You don't say `/getUser/123` — instead, you say `GET /users/123`. This separates identity from action.

Think of it like a filing cabinet analogy: the drawer label (URL path) tells you where to find the document, and your action (GET, PUT, DELETE) tells you what to do with it. For **hierarchical resources** like orders belonging to users, you nest path variables: `/users/{userId}/orders/{orderId}`. This shows the ownership relationship directly in the URL structure. Spring MVC's **@PathVariable** annotation binds these URL segments to method parameters, making the controller code clean and intuitive.

sections.title: RESTful URL Design Rules
sections.content:
amber|Nouns not verbs|~Resources, not actions|/users not /getUsers|HTTP verb = the action|GET/POST/PUT/DELETE
blue|Hierarchy|~Nest related resources|/users/{id}/orders|path = identity|keep it shallow
emerald|Plurals + lowercase|~Consistent naming|/orders/{id}|hyphens for words|/order-items
rose|Trap|~Verbs in the path|/createUser|/deleteOrder|breaks REST conventions

sections.title: RESTful User Resource with Full CRUD Operations
When to Use Path Variables for Resource Design
sections.content:
Use path variables when identifying a **specific resource instance** in a collection: `/products/{productId}` to get product 42.

Use **hierarchical paths** when modeling ownership or parent-child relationships: `/customers/{customerId}/invoices/{invoiceId}` shows that invoice 789 belongs to customer 123. For **filtering or searching** across multiple resources, use query parameters instead: `/products?category=electronics&minPrice=100`. Path variables are for identity, query params are for filtering. In RESTful APIs, path structure should mirror your domain model's relationships. If users own orders, and orders contain items, your URLs reflect that: `/users/{userId}/orders/{orderId}/items/{itemId}`. This makes the API self-documenting and intuitive for client developers.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using verbs in URLs**: Writing `/createUser` or `/getOrderDetails` violates REST principles. The HTTP method is the verb — use `POST /users` and `GET /orders/{id}` instead. Freshers often copy SOAP or RPC patterns where actions are in the URL.
- **Mixing path variables with verbs**: Creating URLs like `/users/{userId}/delete` when it should be `DELETE /users/{userId}`. The HTTP method already expresses the action.
- **Flat URLs for hierarchical data**: Using `/orders/{orderId}` when orders belong to users. The URL `/users/{userId}/orders/{orderId}` better expresses the domain relationship and allows proper access control checks (does this order belong to this user?).

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Nouns not verbs**: URLs identify resources (nouns), HTTP methods define actions (verbs) — GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
**Path variables for identity**: Use {id} segments to identify specific resource instances like /products/42 or /customers/7
**Hierarchical paths**: Model ownership with nested paths like /users/{userId}/orders/{orderId} to show parent-child relationships
**HTTP method semantics**: GET retrieves, POST creates, PUT updates, DELETE removes — the method tells you the action
**Collection vs instance**: /users returns all users (collection), /users/123 returns one user (instance)
**@PathVariable binding**: Spring automatically extracts {userId} from the URL and binds it to method parameters
**Query params for filtering**: Use ?status=active&sort=date for search criteria, not path variables

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When you design RESTful URLs, you follow a simple rule: the URL is a noun that identifies the resource, and the HTTP method is the verb that defines the action. So instead of writing something like slash-get-user-slash-one-two-three, you'd write GET slash-users-slash-one-two-three. The path variable here is the user ID, and GET is the action. For a complete resource, you'd have GET slash-users to list all users, POST slash-users to create a new user, GET slash-users-slash-id to retrieve one user, PUT slash-users-slash-id to update that user, and DELETE slash-users-slash-id to remove it. That's your full CRUD design right there. Now, when you have hierarchical data, you nest the path variables. If orders belong to users, you'd use slash-users-slash-user-id-slash-orders-slash-order-id. This shows the relationship directly in the URL. Spring's at-Path-Variable annotation pulls these values out automatically and binds them to your controller method parameters. One common mistake freshers make is putting verbs in the URL, like slash-delete-order or slash-create-user. That's not RESTful. The HTTP method already tells you the action. Another mistake is using flat URLs when you have hierarchical data. If you just use slash-orders-slash-id, you lose the context of which user owns that order. The nested path gives you better security and clearer semantics. When designing your API, think about your domain model's relationships and mirror them in the URL structure. It makes the API intuitive and self-documenting for anyone using it.

speakable_v2.hook: RESTful URL design has a simple core rule: nouns in the path, verbs in the HTTP method. That one rule eliminates most bad URL patterns.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: RESTful URL design uses the URL to identify a resource and the HTTP method to express the action. The path tells you what you're operating on. GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE tell you what you're doing to it.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: GET /users — list all users.
POST /users — create a new user.
GET /users/{id} — get one user.
PUT /users/{id} — replace a user.
DELETE /users/{id} — remove a user.
GET /users/{userId}/orders — list a user's orders.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: Use plural nouns: /users not /user. Use lowercase and hyphens for multi-word paths: /user-profiles not /userProfiles. Query parameters are for filtering and pagination — /users?status=active — not for defining a different resource.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: candidates miss: /getUser, /deleteOrder, /createProduct are all anti-patterns. They put the action in the URL instead of the HTTP method. Interviewers from companies with public APIs — Amazon, Microsoft — specifically test this because it's a signal of REST maturity.

speakable_v2.cap: Keep nesting to two levels maximum. /users/{id}/orders is clean. /users/{uId}/orders/{oId}/items/{iId}/details is not — flatten it.
